## 2.4 Vision Transformers

### 2.4.1 Motivation and Trade-offs

**The Paradigm Shift**: Transformers learn spatial relationships through self-attention rather than hard-coded convolutions.

**Key Trade-offs**:

| Aspect | CNNs | Vision Transformers |
|--------|------|---------------------|
| **Inductive bias** | Strong (locality, translation equivariance) | Minimal (learns from data) |
| **Data requirements** | Sample-efficient (100K-1M images) | Data-hungry (10M+ images) |
| **Receptive field** | Grows gradually with depth | Global from layer 1 |
| **Complexity** | $O(HW)$ (linear in resolution) | $O((HW)^2)$ (quadratic) |
| **Best use** | Small datasets, real-time, edge | Large-scale pre-training, global context |

**Interview Context**: Companies like Meta (SAM, DINO), Google (ViT), OpenAI (CLIP) use transformers as foundation model backbones. Understanding when CNNs still win is crucial for system design.

---

### 2.4.2 Vision Transformer (ViT, 2020)

**Core Idea**: Treat image as sequence of patches, apply standard Transformer encoder.

**Architecture**:

**1. Patch Embedding**:
- Split 224×224 image into 16×16 patches → 196 patches
- Flatten each patch: $(16 \times 16 \times 3) = 768$ dimensions
- Linear projection to embedding dimension $D$ (typically 768)
- Add learnable position embeddings
- Prepend $[\text{CLS}]$ token for classification

**2. Transformer Encoder** ($L$ layers):
```
z' = MSA(LayerNorm(z)) + z
z  = MLP(LayerNorm(z')) + z'
```

**Multi-Head Self-Attention**:
$$\text{Attention}(\mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V}) = \text{softmax}\left(\frac{\mathbf{QK}^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) \mathbf{V}$$

**3. Classification**: MLP head on $[\text{CLS}]$ token → class logits

**Complexity**: $O(N^2 \cdot D)$ per layer, where $N = (H/P)^2$ patches.

---

**ViT Variants and Performance**:

| Model | Layers | Dim | Heads | Params | ImageNet (pre-trained on JFT-300M) |
|-------|--------|-----|-------|--------|-------------------------------------|
| ViT-Base/16 | 12 | 768 | 12 | 86M | 84.2% |
| ViT-Large/16 | 24 | 1024 | 16 | 307M | 85.2% |
| ViT-Huge/14 | 32 | 1280 | 16 | 632M | 88.5% |

**The Data Hunger Problem**:
- ImageNet-1K only: 76.5% (worse than ResNet-152)
- ImageNet-21K (14M): 85.3% 
- JFT-300M: 88.4%

**Why?** No inductive bias—must learn spatial relationships from data. With enough data, this flexibility becomes an advantage.

---

### 2.4.3 DeiT: Data-Efficient Training (2021)

**Innovation**: Knowledge distillation enables training on ImageNet-1K only.

**Method**: Add distillation token alongside $[\text{CLS}]$ token.

**Loss**:
$$\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(y, \hat{y}_{\text{cls}}) + \alpha \mathcal{L}_{\text{CE}}(y, \hat{y}_{\text{dist}}) + \beta \mathcal{L}_{\text{KD}}(y_{\text{teacher}}, \hat{y}_{\text{dist}})$$

**Key Findings**:

- CNN teacher (RegNetY-16GF) works better than Transformer teacher
- Achieves 81.8% on ImageNet-1K without external pre-training
- Inference: Can use $(\hat{y}_{\text{cls}} + \hat{y}_{\text{dist}})/2$ for best performance

**Impact**: Democratized ViT training—no need for web-scale datasets.

---

### 2.4.4 Swin Transformer (2021)

**Problem**: ViT's $O(N^2)$ doesn't scale to high-resolution or dense prediction tasks.

**Solution**: Hierarchical architecture with windowed attention.

#### Key Mechanisms

**1. Patch Merging** (like CNN pooling):

- Concatenate 2×2 neighbors (4C channels)
- Linear projection: $4C → 2C$
- Result: 4× fewer tokens, 2× channels

**2. Window Attention (W-MSA)**:

- Partition into $M \times M$ non-overlapping windows (typically $M=7$)
- Self-attention within each window only
- Complexity: $O(hw \cdot M^2)$ — **linear in image size**

**3. Shifted Window Attention (SW-MSA)**:

- Alternate between regular and shifted ($M/2$ offset) window partitions
- Enables cross-window communication
- Implemented efficiently via cyclic shift + masking

**Architecture** (4 stages):
```
Input (224×224×3)
→ Patch Partition → (56×56, 96ch)
→ Stage 1: Swin Blocks → (56×56, 96ch)
→ Patch Merge → (28×28, 192ch)
→ Stage 2: Swin Blocks → (28×28, 192ch)
→ Patch Merge → (14×14, 384ch)
→ Stage 3: Swin Blocks → (14×14, 384ch)
→ Patch Merge → (7×7, 768ch)
→ Stage 4: Swin Blocks → (7×7, 768ch)
```

**Performance**:

| Task | Metric | ResNet-50 | ViT-Base | Swin-Tiny | Swin-Base |
|------|--------|-----------|----------|-----------|-----------|
| ImageNet | Top-1 | 76.2% | 77.9% | 81.3% | 83.5% |
| COCO Det | Box AP | 38.0 | - | 42.2 | 46.9 |

**Why Swin Excels**:
- Linear complexity → handles high-resolution
- Hierarchical features → compatible with FPN for detection
- Local windows → preserves fine spatial details

---

### 2.4.5 DETR: Detection Transformer (2020)

**Paradigm**: Treat detection as **direct set prediction** (no anchors, no NMS).

**Architecture**:
```
Image → CNN Backbone → Flatten + Positional Encoding
      → Transformer Encoder (6 layers)
      → Transformer Decoder (6 layers, 100 object queries)
      → Prediction Heads → {class, bbox} × 100
```

**Object Queries**: 100 learnable embeddings that "search" for objects via cross-attention to encoder features.

#### Training with Bipartite Matching

**Hungarian Algorithm** finds optimal one-to-one matching between predictions and ground truth:
$$\sigma^* = \arg\min_{\sigma} \sum_{j} \left[-\hat{p}_{c_j}(\sigma(j)) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{box}}(\hat{\mathbf{b}}_{\sigma(j)}, \mathbf{b}_j)\right]$$

**Loss**:
$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{j} \left[-\log \hat{p}_{c_j}(\sigma^*(j)) + \lambda_{\text{L1}}\|\hat{\mathbf{b}} - \mathbf{b}\|_1 + \lambda_{\text{GIoU}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{GIoU}}\right]$$

**Key Innovation**: Set prediction with matching → **NMS unnecessary** (each object predicted once).

**Performance**: 42.0 AP on COCO (ResNet-101), but requires 500 epochs to converge.

---

### 2.4.6 Deformable DETR (2021)

**Problem**: DETR is slow (500 epochs) and struggles with small objects.

**Solution - Deformable Attention**:
- Attend to only $K=4$ learned reference points (vs. all $N$ pixels)
- Multi-scale sampling from feature pyramid

**Complexity**: $O(N_q \cdot K \cdot D)$ where $K$ is constant → **linear** vs. DETR's $O(N_q \cdot N_k \cdot D)$.

**Deformable Attention**:
$$\text{DeformAttn}(\mathbf{q}, \mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}}) = \sum_{m=1}^M \sum_{k=1}^K \alpha_{mk} \cdot \text{Sample}(\mathbf{p}_{\text{ref}} + \Delta \mathbf{p}_{mk})$$

where $\Delta \mathbf{p}_{mk}$ are learned offsets.

**Multi-Scale**: Sample from multiple FPN levels → better small object detection.

**Performance**:

| Model | Epochs | AP | AP_S (small) |
|-------|--------|-----|--------------|
| DETR | 500 | 40.6 | 20.5 |
| Deformable DETR | 50 | 46.2 | 28.8 |

**Key**: 10× faster training, +8.3 AP on small objects.

---

### 2.4.7 Segment Anything Model (SAM, 2023)

**Vision**: Foundation model for segmentation—segment any object from any prompt, zero-shot.

#### Architecture

**Three Components**:
1. **Image Encoder**: ViT-Huge (632M params, MAE pre-trained)
   - Input: 1024×1024 → Output: 64×64×256 embedding
   - Runs once per image (heavy)

2. **Prompt Encoder** (lightweight):
   - Points/boxes → positional encodings
   - Masks → small CNN
   - Text → CLIP encoder

3. **Mask Decoder**: 2-layer Transformer
   - Outputs 3 masks (whole, part, subpart) + IoU scores
   - Handles ambiguity

**Design**: Heavy encoder (detailed features) + light decoder (real-time interaction).

#### The SA-1B Dataset

**Scale**: 11M images, 1.1B masks (~100 masks/image)

**Three-Stage Data Engine**:
1. **Model-assisted** (4.3M): Humans refine SAM predictions
2. **Semi-automatic** (5.9M): SAM auto-detects, humans fill gaps
3. **Fully automatic** (1.1B): 32×32 grid prompts → filter by confidence + stability

**Key**: Model-in-the-loop—SAM improves, enables more automation, generates more data.

#### Zero-Shot Transfer

**Evaluated on 23 datasets** without fine-tuning:

| Task | Performance |
|------|-------------|
| Single-point segmentation | Outperforms task-specific SOTA |
| Instance segmentation (box prompt) | 94% of fully-supervised ViTDet |
| Edge detection | Competitive with supervised methods |

**Applications**: Photo editing, medical imaging, robotics, video tracking.

**Interview Note**: SAM demonstrates scaling enables generalization in vision (like GPT for language). Companies: Meta (products), MedSAM (medical), robotics startups.

---

## 2.4.8 Summary and Interview Preparation

### Core Concepts Checklist

**Architecture**:
- [ ] ViT patch embedding and $O(N^2)$ complexity
- [ ] Swin windowed attention: $O(N)$ complexity
- [ ] DETR set prediction with Hungarian matching
- [ ] Deformable attention: sparse sampling with learned offsets

**Key Trade-offs**:
- [ ] ViT vs. CNN: data requirements, inductive bias
- [ ] When transformers outperform CNNs (and vice versa)
- [ ] Swin vs. ViT: hierarchical vs. flat, efficient vs. simple

**Applications**:
- [ ] DeiT for limited data scenarios
- [ ] Swin for detection/segmentation backbones
- [ ] DETR family for end-to-end detection
- [ ] SAM for zero-shot segmentation

### Common Interview Questions

1. **"Why does ViT need more data than ResNet?"**
   - No built-in locality/translation equivariance → must learn from data

2. **"How does Swin achieve linear complexity?"**
   - Window attention: $O(M^2)$ per window, $O(hw \cdot M^2)$ total vs. ViT's $O((hw)^2)$

3. **"Why doesn't DETR need NMS?"**
   - Bipartite matching ensures one-to-one assignment → no duplicate predictions

4. **"Deformable DETR vs. DETR trade-offs?"**
   - 10× faster training, better small objects, slightly more complex architecture

5. **"When to use transformer vs. CNN backbone?"**
   - **Transformer**: Large pre-trained models available, global context critical
   - **CNN**: Limited data, real-time constraints, edge deployment

### Interview Preparation Tips

- **Complexity analysis**: Know exact scaling (ViT: $O(N^2)$, Swin: $O(N)$, Deformable: $O(K)$ where $K$ constant)
- **Architecture comparisons**: Multi-dimensional trade-offs (accuracy, speed, memory, data)
- **Recent advances**: DINOv2, SAM 2 (video), Depth Anything
- **Company context**: Meta (SAM, DINO), Google (ViT, Swin), OpenAI (CLIP), Tesla (BEV transformers)

### Further Reading

- [ViT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929) • [Swin](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14030) • [DETR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.12872) • [SAM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.02643)

This completes Vision Transformers—the evolution from pure self-attention (ViT) to efficient hierarchical designs (Swin) to sparse adaptive attention (Deformable DETR) to foundation models (SAM) over 2020-2023.
